The dynamic reversed itself: on the night of Ramchandra Ray’s escape, Sitaram was the palace guard who stopped Udayaditya, disarmed him, and bound him, preventing him from leaving. On the night of Udayaditya’s own escape, Sitaram instead went to Udayaditya in the burning prison and helped him escape, carrying him out and leading him to safety.

Pratapaditya’s initial plan was to send two Pathan men to kill his uncle Basanta Ray when Basanta took shelter at the inn in Simultali on his way to Jessore; it failed. The final method was Muktiyar Khan killing Basanta Ray with a sword on Pratapaditya’s order.

The forged petition was stamped with the Yubaraj's seal, using the signet ring that Rukmini had brought, which had the Yubaraj's name engraved on it, and this was used as evidence to justify Udayaditya's imprisonment.

Ramchandra’s midnight escape led Udayaditya to secretly arrange stipends for the dismissed guards, which eventually reached Pratapaditya; after Pratapaditya ordered the stipends stopped and learned of Surma’s secret actions, he decreed that Surma be exiled.

The song signifies Basanta Ray's loneliness and grief. He sings it in two contrasting contexts: first, alone in Raigarh, feeling desolate and abandoned; second, in Jessore, when he sings it to Vibha but finds the room empty, so he still feels left behind.

Rukmini failed to stop Udayaditya from escaping, so Udayaditya survived; Sitaram later set the prison on fire and spread the rumor of Udayaditya’s death, which led Pratapaditya to order the death sentence for Basanta Ray, the King of Raigarh, and Basanta Ray was killed.

Pratapaditya initially received Ramchandra Ray calmly, without showing joy or haste, while Ramchandra later addressed Pratapaditya’s status in his own court by mocking and belittling him, comparing his royal lineage unfavorably.
She re-enters through the poison prepared by Mangala, which was given to the palace and used to kill Surma.

Udayaditya’s early lament culminated in his formal renunciation of the throne when, after being brought before his father Pratapaditya as a prisoner, he declared that he was not worthy of the kingdom and did not want it, asked for release from the throne, and then took an oath to Ma-Kali, touching her feet, swearing he would never accept even an iota of the kingdom, never sit on the throne, and never touch the royal scepter.

The Mahishi intercepted the letter, and later when Basanta Ray came to Pratapaditya, the Mahishi gave Basanta Ray the letter. After Basanta Ray read it, he and the Mahishi told Vibha that Ramchandra had written a letter requesting that she be sent to Chandradwip, which led Vibha to feel relieved.

Pratapaditya’s plan to trap Ramchandra Ray by blocking the canal with large sal wood logs failed because Rammohan and his followers pulled the boat up and over the logs, allowing Ramchandra to escape.

Basanta Ray's beloved sitar reflects his growing despair because it was his eternal companion and source of joy; as Udayaditya's suffering worsened, Basanta Ray could no longer play or tune it properly, left it behind, and felt utterly alone, singing, “I alone am left behind.”
Earlier, Udayaditya was willing to intervene on behalf of his oppressed subjects, but after Surma’s death, he became fearful and hesitant, and no longer intervened.

In Jessore, when preparing to receive Ramchandra Ray, Vibha was dressed by the Mahishi with eight thick gold bangles and a huge diamond bracelet on each arm, a large nose ring, and styled hair; she was shy, joyful, and flustered under the heavy adornment.

In Chandradwip, when she finally sought Ramchandra Ray, Vibha was dressed as a common woman, veiled her head, and entered the palace like a maidservant or beggar woman, presenting herself with humility and surrender—saying she had come to give away everything and take her leave.

So her attire shifted from elaborate royal/jewel-heavy adornment to plain/common clothing, and her presentation shifted from joyful, shy, adorned queen to shame-ridden, humble, surrendering beggar-like figure.
In his bedchamber, the window symbolized his hope and waiting for Surma. In the prison cell, the window symbolized freedom and his connection to the outside world.

The dynamic began as a flirtatious financial arrangement in which Sitaram borrowed money from Rukmini, and their exchanges included teasing, feigned affection, and joking about repayment and interest. Over time, however, Rukmini’s desperation over the Yubaraj’s imprisonment and Sitaram’s involvement turned the relationship deadly. Later, after the fire and Sitaram’s alleged role in the Yubaraj’s death, Rukmini came to her cottage trembling and threatening. She declared she would lay Sitaram and the Yubaraj in the oven, smear ash on her body for Yama, and then seek vengeance. When Sitaram tried to feign affection, Rukmini became enraged, searched for a curved blade, struck the floor where he had stood, and vowed to make him pay. Sitaram ultimately fled, realizing the encounter had become life-threatening.

Sitaram first used the fire as a simple distraction to help Udayaditya escape, but then his men intentionally set the prison cell on fire and spread the story that the Yubaraj had died in the fire, turning the distraction into a full-fledged cover-up of Udayaditya’s escape.

Ramchandra Ray did not feel grateful; he believed Udayaditya had saved him for the sake of his own sister, not for him, and that it was bound to happen. In his own court, he laughed and joked about Udayaditya’s protective actions without care.

The Emperor of Delhi's threat was initially dismissed by Pratapaditya, but later Bhagavat forged a petition in the Emperor's name and delivered it to Pratapaditya, which Pratapaditya used as a mechanism to imprison his son.

The grooming of Vibha’s hair served as a marker of Surma’s presence because Surma used to style it for Vibha, and when Vibha secretly got her hair done her own way, the Mahishi noticed and believed Surma had purposely ruined it out of jealousy. Later, when Surma was absent, Vibha waited for Surma to braid her hair, sitting quietly as if Surma would come at any moment; but when evening fell and Surma did not come, Vibha’s hair remained unbraided. This unbraided hair thus became a sign of Surma’s tragic absence.
